data.title: Lichen planus pigmentosus — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 8 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen planus pigmentosus** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP)?**
- Variant of LP seen mainly in darker skin (India, Middle East, Latin America) with insidious, persistent dark-brown to slate-grey or blue-grey macules on sun-exposed face and neck or flexures, with little or no itch; now grouped under 'acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation' (ADMH) with ashy dermatosis and pigmented contact dermatitis

**Q2. Triggers.**
- Mustard oil, amla (Indian gooseberry) oil and other hair oils, hair dyes (PPD), henna, fragrances, cosmetics, UV light, hepatitis C, nickel; association with frontal fibrosing alopecia, acrochordons, thyroid disease

**Q3. Clinical patterns.**
- Diffuse, reticulate, blotchy, perifollicular macules
- Sites: forehead, temples, preauricular, neck (most common), upper limbs; inverse LPP — axillae, groin, submammary (lighter-skinned Asians)
- Linear/zosteriform/segmental variants; oral mucosa occasionally; classic LP papules in ~20%

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Vacuolar basal degeneration, sparse lichenoid/perivascular infiltrate, prominent pigment incontinence with many dermal melanophages; atrophic epidermis
- Late lesions: only melanophages (similar to ashy dermatosis/PIH)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Ashy dermatosis/erythema dyschromicum perstans (trunk, grey-blue, active red border in early stage, Latin American), Riehl's melanosis (pigmented contact dermatitis — patch test positive), melasma (brown, symmetrical, cheeks, no grey), drug-induced pigmentation, FDE (recurrent, sharp), macular amyloidosis (rippled, back), acanthosis nigricans (velvety, flexures), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, exogenous ochronosis, nevus of Ota/Hori

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Dermoscopy (blue-grey dots/globules in perifollicular and speckled patterns), biopsy; patch test (cosmetic, hair-oil and dye series); HCV serology; thyroid function

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Avoid triggers (stop mustard/amla oil, PPD dyes, fragrances); strict photoprotection (including visible light)
- Topical tacrolimus 0.1%, short courses of topical steroids, depigmenting agents (azelaic acid, kojic acid, hydroquinone short-term — limited effect on dermal pigment)
- Systemic: oral tranexamic acid, low-dose isotretinoin, oral mini-pulse steroids (active disease), dapsone, hydroxychloroquine (limited evidence)
- Lasers: Q-switched Nd:YAG low-fluence, picosecond — variable; risk of worsening
- Counsel chronicity

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic, slowly progressive or stable for years; spontaneous fading rare; major cosmetic and psychosocial burden

## Quick spotter facts
- Slate-grey facial and neck pigmentation in a user of mustard/amla oil — LPP
- Pigment incontinence with sparse lichenoid infiltrate

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen planus pigmentosus; acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
